title: Pauri 1, meaning: joy, mother
hookLine: joy, mother, I have found the True Guru, easily, and the songs of joy are sung (Anand 1)
tomorrow: Stay with the Lord, my mind

lines: A BABY IS BORN; THE PHONE RINGS.
cards: A baby is born in a Punjabi family, and within the hour the phone is ringing. Then the doorbell. Aunties arrive with sweets.
Uncles arrive with more sweets. Someone puts music on. Everyone keeps saying one word to the parents, the grandparents, anyone standing still long enough: vadhaiyan!
Congratulations! It's the word for news so good the whole family turns up. The first pauri of Anand Sahib has that word in it: a party in five lines, and the guests are not who you'd expect.

teach.b: Here's the pauri, in paraphrase. Joy has come, my mother, for I have found the True Guru.
I found the True Guru with ease, and my mind rings with congratulations.
The jewel-like ragas, with their families, have come to sing the Word.

teach.h: SING THE WORD, ALL OF YOU.
teach.b: Sing the Word of the Lord, all you who have set it in your minds. Says Nanak, bliss has come; I have found the True Guru. Take the pieces.
First, mother: the news goes to the person you'd tell first. Then sahaj, with ease. Sahaj is a big word in Sikh thought: a natural, settled ease, the opposite of straining.
The Guru wasn't won by force; the joy came the way sleep comes. Then the party. Vaadhaaeeaa, congratulations, the same word aunties call out at a birth.
And who shows up? The ragas.

In old Indian music lore, ragas were pictured with families and companions, so the pauri pictures the musical modes themselves arriving at the door like relatives, ready to sing: joy so big the music turns up in person.
Then a turn outward: sing the Word, all of you who've taken it in. The joy doesn't stay private. Notice what this pauri isn't.

It isn't a lecture about joy. It's a report of joy, from inside it, still breathless. That's what Guru Amar Das gives Sikhs to sing at the close of their gatherings: not an idea about bliss, but good news.

how: The first pauri of Anand Sahib is sung at the close of Sikh gatherings, from weddings to ordinary services.

o: strict effort that wins the Guru by force
a sudden burst of wild excitement
a natural, settled ease, not straining

s: in the pauri, the Guru is found through great struggle
sahaj setee: with ease, the way sleep comes.
the pauri pictures the ragas arriving with their families to sing
joy so big the music itself turns up at the door.
the first pauri keeps the joy private
it turns outward: sing the Word, all you who have set it in your minds.

games.q: joy has come and the mind is ringing with congratulations. in the pauri, who arrives to celebrate?
o: the jewel-like ragas, with their families, to sing the Word.
no one: the joy is kept secret.
games.why: raag ratan parvaar pareeaa: the jewel-like ragas and their families come to sing. the music itself shows up like relatives at a birth.

practice: Let your mind go over the last few days and find one piece of good news, any size: a friend's recovery, a finished project, a small win nobody noticed.
Feel it again from inside, the way the pauri does, as news worth carrying to the first person you'd tell. If you pray, you can thank the Guru with Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Sahaj, natural ease. Joy has come, my mother: the Guru found with sahaj, the mind ringing with congratulations, and the ragas arriving like family to sing.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sahaj, natural ease and poise; in pauri 1, the Guru is found with sahaj.

carryVoice: Your line: joy, mother. Some news is too good to keep in one room. Three hundred eighty-two days, and counting.
